channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Russia's war pressed on Europe: a missile strike killed ten in the Kharkiv region, French prosecutors opened an interference probe over the 2027 election, and Moscow courted energy deals in Myanmar.
item.description:
At least ten people were killed and eight injured in a Russian missile strike on Petschenihy in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, damaging civilian infrastructure. Beyond the front, the war's political dimension widened: the Paris prosecutor's office opened an investigation into suspected Russian interference targeting French politicians Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal — both contenders for the 2027 presidential race — following an earlier probe into Raphaël Glucksmann; Russia denied interfering. Moscow, meanwhile, deepened ties elsewhere, with President Putin saying Russian companies are ready to join hydrocarbon exploration and a refinery project in Myanmar, and Russia's last opposition party, Yabloko, lost its court appeal against exclusion from September's parliamentary elections. Separately, EU railway regulators — with Swiss input — agreed stricter freight-wagon safety rules after the 2023 Gotthard tunnel derailment.

Industry Impact

The continued war sustains Europe's energy-security premium and the risk of further sanctions and counter-sanctions that complicate raw-material and logistics flows. Election-interference concerns raise the odds of political volatility in France, the euro area's second-largest economy, over the next 18 months — a source of policy and demand uncertainty. For manufacturers the practical read is that the Russia-linked risk backdrop (energy, sanctions, political stability) remains a standing feature of European planning rather than a fading one.

Handelsblatt | TF1 INFO | AA | Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: A ratings agency cut India's 2026-27 growth forecast to 6.8% on Middle East and weather risks, even as New Delhi advanced a free-trade deal with Israel, expanded semiconductor plans and leased US Navy drones.
item.description:
India Ratings & Research trimmed its forecast for India's growth in the 2026-27 fiscal year to 6.8%, down from 7.6% the year before, citing fuel and food inflation from the West Asia (Middle East) conflict, a weak rupee and El Niño weather risks. Even so, India kept building strategic and trade links: free-trade talks with Israel are moving into the market-access phase, with both sides preparing to exchange offers; three semiconductor projects under the India Semiconductor Mission may go live by end-2026, with Semicon India 2026 opening on 17 September; and the Defence Ministry signed a INR 19.43 billion deal to lease two US-built MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones for the navy. The mix shows a still-fast-growing economy hedging external risks through diversified partnerships.

Industry Impact

India remains one of the strongest structural demand stories for ACS producers, tied to construction, autos and a fast-expanding electronics and semiconductor base. A trimmed but still-high 6.8% growth rate keeps that trajectory intact, while new chip fabs create demand for specialty chemicals and materials. The Israel FTA and defence deals point to widening industrial supply chains that suppliers can position around. The main watch-item is imported inflation from oil, which raises input costs and could pressure margins in price-sensitive Indian end-markets.

Business Standard | The Hindu Business Line | The Hindu Business Line | Business Standard

item.title: UK unemployment rose to 4.9%, the Treasury modelled growth as low as 0.3% in 2027 if the Iran war keeps disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, and Washington called its threat of a 100% tariff over Britain's digital-services tax no bluff.
item.description:
UK unemployment held at 4.9% in the three months to June, above the 4.8% economists expected, while pay growth slowed and vacancies fell — a cooling labour market that, one economist argued, removes the need for a Bank of England rate rise unless energy prices spike sharply. Internal Treasury modelling seen by government sources suggests UK GDP could grow as little as 0.3% in 2027 if disruption to the Strait of Hormuz linked to the Iran war persists to the end of 2026. On trade, the US trade representative said Trump's threat to impose a 100% import tariff on the UK over its digital-services tax — a 2% levy on big US tech firms that raised about GBP 800 million in 2024/25 — is "not a bluff." The combination points to a softening economy exposed to both energy and trade shocks.

Industry Impact

A weaker UK labour market and downgraded growth path dampen construction and industrial demand for ACS products in one of Europe's larger markets. The digital-services-tax dispute is a reminder that tariff risk now reaches services and can spill into goods: a 100% US tariff, if enacted, would disrupt UK-US trade broadly. Manufacturers with UK exposure should factor a slower domestic economy and the tail risk of a transatlantic tariff escalation into demand planning.

AA | The Guardian | Herald Scotland | The Independent

item.title: A global retreat in AI shares dragged Asian chip stocks lower — the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell nearly 5% and TSMC's US shares dropped 4% — even as AI demand lifted Taiwan's growth toward a multi-decade high.
item.description:
A pullback in artificial-intelligence stocks rippled through Asian markets. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) fell nearly 5%, TSMC's US-listed shares dropped about 4%, and Taiwan index futures slid 1.24% in overnight trading, while Hong Kong and mainland tech shares also declined as investors rotated out of AI names and into energy. Yet the underlying Taiwan economy is running hot on the same AI theme: second-quarter GDP growth reached 12.92%, and forecasters see full-year growth of 9–10%, among the highest in decades, on AI-server and chip demand. Taiwan even plans NT$10,000 cash handouts to share the gains in 2027. The split — frothy equities cooling while real AI-driven output surges — captures a market weighing whether the AI investment boom is running ahead of its payoff.

Industry Impact

Semiconductor and electronics manufacturing is a significant end-market for specialty adhesives, coatings and cleaning chemistries, so Taiwan's real-economy AI boom supports demand for those high-value products regardless of short-term equity swings. The equity wobble matters mainly as a signal of sentiment risk: a sharp AI-market correction could slow the capital-expenditure plans that drive chip-fab construction and tool orders. For now the divergence favours suppliers exposed to actual fab build-out over those tied to market sentiment.

Chinatimes.com | The Economic Times | Commercial Times | The Nation

item.title: A survey of over 2,000 mainland Chinese firms found 82% plan to expand existing overseas operations and 91% intend to enter ASEAN markets, as Chinese manufacturers accelerate a push abroad.
item.description:
A Hong Kong Trade Development Council survey of more than 2,000 mainland companies found 82% intend to scale up their existing overseas operations and 63% want to develop new foreign business, with 94% eyeing Belt and Road markets and 91% specifically planning a presence in Southeast Asia — Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam most often named. Separate data reinforced the pull of the region: approved foreign investment in Thailand rose 37% in the first seven months of 2026, with Singapore and Chinese investors prominent. Chinese industrial-robot maker Estun's move into Germany shows the same outward drive reaching developed markets. The trend reflects firms diversifying production and sales away from a soft home market and around US tariff walls, increasingly through third countries.

Industry Impact

The relocation of Chinese manufacturing into ASEAN reshapes where adhesives, coatings and sealants demand grows — and where competition intensifies. New Chinese-owned plants in Southeast Asia create fresh local demand for industrial ACS inputs, an opportunity for suppliers with regional footprints. At the same time, routing production through third countries is exactly what Washington's "transshipment" crackdown targets, so supply chains built around ASEAN assembly carry rising trade-policy risk that customers and suppliers should factor into sourcing decisions.

South China Morning Post | Xinhua | The Standard | China Economic Net

item.title: To offset weak demand and a housing slump, China issued an 18-point plan to lift consumption in smaller cities and counties and set green-industry and logistics goals under its next five-year plan.
item.description:
China's Ministry of Commerce and eight other departments released an 18-measure guideline to energise "lower-tier" markets — the counties and smaller cities where much of the population lives — by upgrading retail channels, encouraging brands to expand there, promoting trade-ins, and boosting rural e-commerce and services. It is aimed squarely at the soft domestic demand shown in July's data. Alongside it, Beijing advanced its 15th Five-Year Plan agenda: a plan to make Shanghai a global supply-chain hub by 2030, a green and low-carbon industrial plan from MIIT, and green-taxation reforms. Several provinces rolled out fresh consumer-goods trade-in subsidies. The thrust is to pull new demand from under-served domestic markets and modern logistics while the property sector stays weak.

Industry Impact

Stronger county-level consumption and trade-in schemes support demand for appliances, vehicles and construction in China's interior — end-markets that use adhesives, coatings and sealants. The supply-chain and logistics upgrades could lower distribution costs for suppliers operating in China. But the green-industry and VOC-tax elements (see the ACS insight) also raise the bar on emissions, so the same plans that expand demand tighten the environmental rules formulators must meet. Net, China is trying to grow domestic volume while pushing its industry up the sustainability curve.

Business Standard | Global Times | Xinhua | China Economic Net

item.title: German data turned more positive: housing permits rose 15.1% in the first half — the strongest since 2016 — investor sentiment jumped, and a cooperative-bank group doubled its 2026 growth forecast to 1.0%.
item.description:
After months of gloom, several German indicators improved together. Building permits for new homes and conversions rose 15.1% year-on-year to 126,300 units in the first half of 2026, the strongest first-half increase since 2016 and a tentative sign of life in a construction sector that has been in a deep slump. The ZEW gauge of investor expectations climbed 7.9 points to 34.2 in August, with the current-situation reading also improving markedly. And the association of cooperative banks (BVR) doubled its 2026 growth forecast for Germany to 1.0% from 0.5%. The improvement is uneven — many permitted housing projects are still being cancelled on high costs — and it sits against continued weakness in industry, but it marks a clear change of tone from the contraction reported in recent alerts.

Industry Impact

Construction is the single biggest demand driver for sealants, adhesives and coatings, so a genuine rebound in German building permits — Europe's largest construction market — is an early positive signal for ACS volumes, even if the recovery in actual completions lags by many months. Improving investor sentiment and a higher growth forecast support the broader industrial demand backdrop. The caveat is that permits are a leading indicator, not orders: high financing and material costs are still cancelling projects, so the read-through to real demand should be treated as cautious optimism.

Handelsblatt | Tagesschau | AA | Handelsblatt

item.title: Extreme heat and drought could erase most of the EU's forecast 2026 growth, French and German officials reported collapsing harvests, and Britain's parched south-east added to a Europe-wide climate hit to output.
item.description:
A report by Dutch bank Triodos warned that this year's extreme heat could wipe out most or all of the EU's expected 2026 growth — the European Commission had forecast 1.1% and the IMF 0.9% before the heatwave — through lost farm output, strained energy and rivers, and reduced labour productivity. On the ground, France's agriculture minister acknowledged a "collapse" in harvests, with maize and fodder crops hit hardest and fresh fruit and vegetable prices up 3.8%, while Germany's minister promised drought aid to farmers as an emergency fund proved too small. Britain's south-east has had virtually no significant rain for two months, drying rivers and browning landscapes across Kent, Sussex and Surrey. The picture is of a slow-building supply and cost shock layered on top of the energy strain from the Iran war.

Industry Impact

Climate-driven farm losses feed through to bio-based feedstocks and to food-and-beverage customers whose demand shapes packaging, adhesives and coatings orders. More directly, drought lowers river levels on freight corridors like the Rhine — a recurring constraint on moving bulk chemicals and raw materials in Europe — and heat can force output curbs at water- and energy-intensive plants. A summer that dents overall EU growth also softens the industrial demand backdrop for ACS products in the region.

The Globe and Mail | Challenges | Die Zeit | BBC News

item.title: Washington tightened its technology decoupling from China: a new FCC rule demands 65% US content for advanced robots, drone tariffs of up to 100% took hold, and Germany opened a drone-defence research centre.
item.description:
The US telecoms regulator, the FCC, added foreign-made "advanced robotic devices" to its Covered List of technology deemed a national-security risk; new models must contain at least 65% US content to be exempt — a bar even a robot marketed as the "most American" does not yet meet. It follows Washington's earlier move to put tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones over 25 kg, those with thermal imaging, and key components, with a lower 25% band for some parts. The security theme extended to Europe: Germany opened a drone-defence research centre at a former East German airfield to detect and neutralise hostile unmanned aircraft after a wave of suspicious sightings over critical infrastructure. Surveys underline the anxiety — 74% of European business leaders worry a cut-off from US technology could disrupt operations, and the UK is assessing the economic hit if Britons lose access to frontier AI models.

Industry Impact

Content-origin rules like the FCC's 65% threshold are a new compliance axis for anyone buying automation hardware: robots and drones may need documented US or allied content to be usable in sensitive settings, complicating procurement for multinationals that source globally. For manufacturers the message is to map the origin of automation equipment now, because national-security lists can strand non-compliant machines. The parallel European drive for "digital sovereignty" also hints at future preference rules favouring EU-sourced technology.

Forbes | MarketScreener | Dawn | Politico Europe

item.title: Humanoid-robot maker Unitree debuted on Shanghai's STAR tech board on 19 August, with retail demand oversubscribed more than 8,000 times, as China's robotics build-out and IPO pipeline accelerated.
item.description:
Unitree Robotics listed on Shanghai's Science and Technology Innovation Board (the STAR Market, China's Nasdaq-style venue for tech firms) on 19 August, selling about 40.45 million shares at CNY 150.80 each to raise roughly CNY 6.1 billion. Retail demand exceeded the shares on offer by more than 8,000 times, a record for the board. The debut sits within a broader surge: another Chinese robotics start-up, Lumos, is preparing a 2027 IPO after raising about CNY 1 billion; the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Center unveiled a "super-brain" system letting robots follow complex language commands and carry out long tasks autonomously; and industrial-robot leader Estun is expanding into Germany's Mittelstand heartland. Reporting also noted that Unitree's most successful robot-dog designs drew on quadruped-movement breakthroughs originally funded by the US military — a reminder of how research crosses borders even as trade walls rise.

Industry Impact

China's robotics scale-up cuts two ways for Western manufacturers. It lowers the cost of automation that chemical and adhesives plants can deploy, but it also builds a formidable Chinese competitor in industrial and humanoid robots — now reaching into European home markets via firms like Estun. For ACS producers, cheaper and more capable robots support the automation of mixing, packaging and quality inspection; strategically, the pace of Chinese capital flowing into "embodied AI" signals where automation cost curves are heading over the next few years.

China Daily | China Economic Net | Global Times | Valor Econômico | The Economic Times

item.title: New EU packaging rules will force recycled content into plastic packaging from 2030 while China and Africa push circular-economy and green-tax measures, adding compliance cost across the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) chain.
item.description:
The regulatory tightening around materials continued. Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) — the bloc's overhaul of packaging law — manufacturers of plastic packaging will face binding minimum recycled-content requirements from 2030, starting at up to 35% depending on packaging type and rising thereafter. That reshapes demand for recyclate and for the adhesives and coatings used in packaging, which must remain compatible with recycled substrates and recycling streams. In parallel, China's draft 15th Five-Year Plan proposes optimising its "green taxation" system, including piloting an environmental-protection tax on volatile organic compounds (VOCs) — the solvents central to many paints and coatings — and MIIT issued a five-year plan for green and low-carbon industry. Africa's Circular Economy Fund extended national roadmaps to eight more countries. Together they show recycled-content mandates and emissions-linked taxes spreading across the major markets that ACS formulators serve.

Industry Impact

For Henkel and its peers the direction is consistent: rising demand for recyclable and low-VOC formulations, and higher cost for products that do not fit circular systems. The PPWR recycled-content rule is a design constraint as much as a compliance task — packaging adhesives and coatings must work with recyclate and not contaminate recycling streams, which favours suppliers who can certify recyclability. A pilot VOC tax in China would raise the cost advantage of water-based and high-solids coatings. Firms that move early on circular-compatible product lines turn these rules into a differentiator rather than a drag.

Handelsblatt | China Economic Net | China Economic Net | AllAfrica

item.title: With no path to end the Iran war, the US energy agency expects oil prices to stay high into early 2027, oil majors booked record quarterly profits, and Gulf producers moved to expand crude storage in Japan and South Korea.
item.description:
The expired US–Iran ceasefire and Tehran's more aggressive stance kept Brent crude climbing for a third straight session, near USD 91.50 a barrel. The US Energy Information Administration said oil production and trade patterns are unlikely to return to pre-conflict normal until early 2027, and expects prices to stay elevated until then. The strain is reshaping supply logistics: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are reportedly seeking to expand their oil reserves stored in Japan and South Korea, hedging against disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, while more than 6,000 seafarers remain stranded in the Gulf. The high-price environment handed oil majors a windfall — ExxonMobil reported second-quarter profit of about USD 14.5 billion (double a year earlier) and Chevron around USD 12.1 billion (nearly five times higher). Analysts said CNN reporting suggests Trump is shifting from seeking a quick deal to sustained economic and military pressure on Iran.

Industry Impact

A "higher for longer" oil outlook into 2027 keeps upward pressure on the naphtha and crude-derived feedstocks behind plastics, solvents and many adhesive raw materials, and on freight. The move by Gulf exporters to pre-position crude in Asia signals they expect the disruption to persist, not fade — so chemical buyers should assume structurally higher and more volatile input costs, keep safety stock rebuilt, and revisit oil-linked surcharge clauses rather than wait for a return to pre-war pricing.

Arab News | The Times of India | Lianhe Zaobao | China Economic Net | The Economic Times

item.title: Hours before new 50% US tariffs on about USD 20 billion of Canadian goods were due on 19 August, Trump said the US and Canada had reached a deal in principle and postponed the duties for three days to finalise the paperwork.
item.description:
After days of brinkmanship, the confrontation eased at the last moment. President Trump had signed an order to impose 50% duties on a wide range of Canadian exports — from cement and lumber to wine, dairy and hockey sticks, covering roughly 5% of Canada's exports to the US — using Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act, a rarely used clause allowing duties on countries judged to discriminate against US commerce. He turned to that older law after courts questioned the emergency powers behind his earlier "reciprocal" tariffs. Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Trump twice in two days, and negotiators explored cutting US duties on Canadian cars to 15% if a minimum share of each vehicle's content is North American, in exchange for Canadian concessions on autos, metals and lumber. Late on 18 August Trump announced a deal had been reached "subject to the finalisation of documents" and pushed the tariff start back by three days. This resolves — at least temporarily — the tariff cliff flagged in recent alerts.

Industry Impact

For construction-linked chemicals the reprieve is welcome: cement, lumber and building materials were squarely on the target list, and duties there feed straight into the construction demand that drives sealants, adhesives and coatings. But the relief is fragile — a three-day extension, not a signed treaty — and the move to Section 338 shows the US will keep tariffs alive on several legal foundations even if courts curb the original basis. Firms with cross-border North American supply chains should treat durable duties as the base case and watch the proposed 15% auto rate as a possible template for sector-by-sector relief.

The Globe and Mail | BBC News | MarketScreener | Financial Post | La Presse
